title: Elements • Book III • Proposition 35
subtitle: Intersecting Chords Theorem
Visual description: Given circle ABCD and intersecting chords AC and BD meeting at E; if E is the center, all four segments are equal radii.
narration: Elements, Book three, Proposition thirty-five. If two chords intersect inside a circle, the rectangle contained by the segments of one chord equals the rectangle contained by the segments of the other. In circle A B C D, let chords A C and B D intersect at point E. We claim that the rectangle A E by E C equals the rectangle D E by E B. If both chords pass through the center E, all four segments A E, E C, D E, and E B are equal radii, so the rectangles contained by them are immediately equal.

subslides.enunciation: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

title: Perpendiculars and Radii from the Center
subtitle: Construction
Visual description: Find the center F of circle ABCD, drop perpendiculars FG to AC and FH to BD, and join radii FB, FC, and segment FE.
narration: Now suppose the chords do not pass through the center. Find the center F of circle A B C D, and draw perpendiculars F G to A C and F H to B D. Join the radii F B and F C, and join segment F E from the center to the intersection of the chords.

title: Equal Rectangles via Difference of Squares
subtitle: Demonstration
Visual description: Apply III.3 and II.5 to express rect(AE, EC) + sq(EG) = sq(GC), add sq(FG) via I.47 to get rect(AE, EC) + sq(FE) = sq(FC) = sq(FB), and subtract sq(FE).
narration: Because F G passes through the center perpendicular to chord A C, it bisects A C at G. Since A C is cut equally at G and unequally at E, Book two Proposition five shows that the rectangle A E by E C plus the square on E G equals the square on G C. Adding the square on F G to both sides, the Pythagorean theorem on right triangles F G E and F G C turns those sums into the square on F E and the square on radius F C. By the exact same reasoning on chord B D, the rectangle D E by E B plus the square on F E equals the square on radius F B. Since radii F C and F B have equal squares, subtracting the common square on F E leaves the rectangle A E by E C equal to the rectangle D E by E B, as was required to prove.

subslides.enunciation: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.

title: Interior Power of a Point & Dependency Graph
subtitle: Commentary & Genealogy
Visual description: Commentary on Euclid's four cases vs. Campanus's unified proof and the interior Power of a Point invariant R^2 - d^2, followed by the G.143 genealogy card.
narration: Euclid proves four cases depending on whether one or neither chord passes through the center, while Campanus condensed the proof into this single general case. Together with Proposition thirty-six, it establishes the interior Power of a Point theorem: for any point E inside a circle of radius R at distance d from the center, the product of the chord segments through E is always R squared minus d squared. In the GEOMETOR dependency graph, Proposition thirty-five synthesizes fifty-seven ancestor nodes across Books one, two, and three—combining chord bisection from Book three Proposition three, the difference-of-squares rectangle identity from Book two Proposition five, and the Pythagorean theorem from Book one Proposition forty-seven.

subslides.enunciation: If in a circle two straight lines cut one another, the rectangle contained by the segments of the one is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments of the other.
subslides.narration: Euclid proves four cases depending on whether one or neither chord passes through the center, while Campanus condensed the proof into this single general case. Together with Proposition thirty-six, it establishes the interior Power of a Point theorem: for any point E inside a circle of radius R at distance d from the center, the product of the chord segments through E is always R squared minus d squared.
subslides.symbolic: rect(/ A E /, / E C /) = rect(/ D E /, / E B /) = sq(R) − sq(/ F E /)
subslides.clause_html: rect(/ A E /, / E C /) = rect(/ D E /, / E B /) = sq(R) − sq(/ F E /)
subslides.commentary_title: Campanus's General Case & Interior Power of a Point
subslides.commentary_body: Euclid separates four cases (both chords through the center; one through the center bisecting the other; one through the center not bisecting the other; neither through the center). As Heath notes, Campanus gave only the last case as necessary because both rect(/ A E /, / E C /) and rect(/ D E /, / E B /) equal sq(R) − sq(/ F E /), establishing the interior Power of a Point invariant.
